records.table: Christian Drouin is a family calvados house of the Pays d'Auge, and its Sélection is the young one built for mixing: cider apples and perry pears, distilled in a column still and kept fresh in old casks. Reach for it in a Widow's Kiss.
records.story: In 1960 the founder took on the Fiefs Sainte-Anne, a farm of cider apple orchards in the hills of Gonneville, near Honfleur. By the house's account he distilled his cider with the help of a licensed distiller from the north of the Pays d'Auge, and laid the spirit down in former sherry, port and calvados casks in the farm's old outbuildings, buying older stocks when other estates were sold. His son joined him in partnership in 1969, but nothing was sold until 1979, once the stocks were judged deep enough: that gap is why some accounts date the house to 1960 and others to about 1980. In the early 1990s production moved to a seventeenth-century farm at Coudray-Rabut, near Pont-l'Évêque, where the press, the stills and the ageing cellars stand together. The founder's grandson joined in 2004, the third generation at the house. The range runs from the young Sélection, column distilled from apples and pears, to Pays d'Auge blends double distilled in pot stills and aged mostly in small casks. For a bartender the Sélection is the house's mixing calvados, the one to pour in the classic apple brandy drinks.

records.story: Père Magloire dates itself to 1821, and Debrise-Dulac, the firm under which the brand grew, is given the same founding year. Its distillery and cellars stand on the road out of Pont-l'Évêque towards Trouville, in the middle of the Pays d'Auge. The appellation on the VSOP has a history of its own. In 1942, with the state requisitioning spirits for the war, the cider brandy of the Pays d'Auge was recognised as an appellation, which set it apart from industrial spirit and spared its stocks; its rules ask for cider of at least 70 per cent apples, double distillation in pot stills and at least two years in oak, and a VSOP must have four. In 2018 the house opened its old cellars at Pont-l'Évêque to visitors as the Calvados Experience, a tour of Norman history that ends in a tasting. For a bartender the VSOP is a calvados a guest will often have met on a shop shelf, and the plain lesson in what Pays d'Auge on a label promises.

records.story: The house was founded in the Pays d'Auge in 1825, and by its own account it double distilled all its calvados from the start: a first pass through the copper pot still makes the brouillis, a low wine, and a second draws the spirit. Its distillery stands at the Moulin de la Foulonnerie at Coquainvilliers, and four generations of the family followed the founder, as the house counts them. The house's claim is that the family pressed for double distillation to be tied to an appellation. In 1942, with the state requisitioning spirits for the war, Calvados Pays d'Auge was recognised as an appellation, and the pot still and the two passes became its rule; the other calvados country was given a lesser status that year and became the Calvados appellation in 1984, which allows a single pass in a column still, and the pear country of Domfront gained its own appellation in 1997. The VSOP is the house's blend of several Pays d'Auge calvados, none younger than four years, married again in cask after blending. For a bartender it is the Pays d'Auge to learn the appellation on: two passes through the still, four years in oak at least, and apple fruit that holds up in a drink.

records.story: Daron is a name on a bottle rather than a distillery a visitor can find. The calvados is made in the Pays d'Auge, and Maison Ferrand, the Cognac house founded in 1989 at Ars in the Charente, is named as its producer; where it is distilled is not disclosed. Ferrand is known behind the bar for bottlings built for old recipes, among them its 1840 Original Formula cognac of 2011, and Daron Fine follows that line: a young, fresh calvados with a light hand of oak, made to be mixed. What the label does disclose is the appellation, and the appellation tells the rest of the story. In 1942, with the state requisitioning spirits for the war, the Pays d'Auge was recognised as an appellation to set its calvados apart from industrial spirit. Its rules ask for cider of at least 70 per cent apples, the rest perry pears, double distillation in pot stills and at least two years in oak. For a bartender Daron Fine is the calvados to shake: its apple stays clear through citrus and sugar, and a Pays d'Auge on the label means the two passes through the still are the law, not a choice.

records.story: By the estate's account, Pierre Groult (1830 to 1918) began distilling his own cider at the Clos de la Hurvanière in 1860; another account puts the start nearer 1850. His son Léon Groult (1874 to 1923) planted orchards, built a second ageing cellar and set up stills for the farm. Roger Groult (1905 to 1988), whose name the label carries, enlarged the distillery, built a large ageing cellar in 1952 and in 1975 made the business a company, Calvados Roger Groult SA. His son Jean-Pierre Groult (1946 to 2008) took the calvados beyond France as an early exporter. Through five generations, as the family counts them, the estate has kept to the old method: antique copper pot stills heated by a wood fire, two distillations, old French oak and a blend the estate calls perpetual. The Réserve, sold as 3 ans d'âge in a newer livery, is where its range begins, and the estate names it for cocktails as well as for after dinner. For a bartender it shows what three years do to Pays d'Auge cider: the apple stays at the front.

others.name: Roger Groult 8 Ans d'Âge
others.note: No calvados in it is younger than eight years; bottled at 41 per cent, with lightly cooked apple, vanilla and cinnamon by the estate's note.

others.name: Roger Groult Vénérable
others.note: No calvados in the blend is younger than eighteen years; baked apple, warm spice and dried fruit by the estate's note.

traps: The bottle long sold as Réserve is called 3 ans d'âge on the estate's shop page, and Reserve 3 years old on its cocktail page; under the calvados rules Réserve promises the same three years.
The estate's fire is wood, under antique copper pot stills: not gas, and not a column still.

cards.prompt: What heats the stills at the Roger Groult estate?
cards.answer: A wood fire, under antique copper pot stills at the Clos de la Hurvanière; the cider is distilled twice.

cards.prompt: Who was the Roger of Roger Groult?
cards.answer: Roger Groult (1905 to 1988), the third generation, who enlarged the distillery and built a large ageing cellar in 1952.

quiz.q: A guest asks what heats the stills at the Roger Groult estate. What does the estate use?
options: A wood fire under the pot
quiz.explain: The estate heats its antique copper pot stills with a wood fire, its old way of working; gas and steam are how many other stills are heated.

quiz.q: In which year did Roger Groult build a large ageing cellar at the Clos de la Hurvanière?
quiz.explain: He built the cellar in 1952; 1975 is the year he made the business a company, and 1860 the year the estate gives for its first distilling.

report: A swap of the bottling is proposed: the estate's own page sells the young bottling as Calvados Pays d'Auge 3 ans d'âge, and a 2020 tasting blog says the Réserve was the old entry blend, replaced by the 3 Ans in a new livery; shops still sell both names. The bottle name keeps the roster's words for the lint; the proposed flagship is Roger Groult Calvados Pays d'Auge 3 Ans d'Âge, with the reason that the estate no longer prints Réserve on its own page. The refuter should read a label photograph.

The plan's why says the Groults have held the Clos since the eighteenth century: the estate's history begins with Pierre Groult distilling in 1860, and Wikipedia says about 1850; neither gives the eighteenth century, so it is left out, and year stays empty because the two do not agree.

The dead are dated from the estate's history page as its search summary gave them (Pierre 1830 to 1918, Léon 1874 to 1923, Roger 1905 to 1988, Jean-Pierre 1946 to 2008), with Wikipedia's article as the second account; the refuter should confirm each pair in Wikipedia itself.
The family's present generation, a brother and his sister who took over in 2022, are living: both are added to people.json and named nowhere.
The strength of the 3 ans is 40 per cent on the estate's sheet; the 8 ans is 41 per cent on its own page. The count of stills (three) and the orchard area (27 hectares) are left out as fixed counts.

The plan's note says all five picks are Pays d'Auge: in fact the Christian Drouin Sélection is plain AOC Calvados, column distilled from apples and pears, so the group does show the broad appellation once. The pear led Domfrontais still has no pick; Christian Drouin's Le Domfrontais stands among that record's other bottlings.
Left out: the estate's prizes and its claims of a world title (no scores), and its prices.

changed: bottle.taste: the estate's own note gives intense, fresh, tart apple with slight wood; the taste now says so rather than casks kept in the background.
